propositions.text: The appellant is a Chinese citizen appealing the RPD decision denying Convention Refugee status.
propositions.quote: XXXX XXXX XXXX is a citizen of China. The Appellant appeals the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision of November 2, 2016, that he is not a Convention Refugee.

propositions.text: RPD found no more than a mere possibility of persecution or risk to life or cruel treatment on a Convention ground.
propositions.quote: The RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that there is not more than a mere possibility that the Appellant would be persecuted for a Convention ground or that it is likely he would be subjected personally to a risk to his life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appellant is a Chinese citizen appealing the RPD's finding that he is not a Convention Refugee due to insufficient risk of persecution or harm.

propositions.text: The appellant requests the RAD to set aside the RPD decision and find him a Convention refugee or refer the claim back for redetermination.
propositions.quote: The Appellant respectfully requests that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD and find that he is a Convention refugee. Alternatively, he submits that the claim should be referred back to the RPD for re-determination.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant requests the RAD to overturn the RPD decision or refer the claim back for re-determination.

propositions.text: Pursuant to IRPA paragraph 111(1)(a), the RAD confirms the RPD decision.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD confirms the RPD decision under IRPA paragraph 111(1)(a).

propositions.text: The appeal raises four issues regarding the RPD's findings on exit from China, being wanted by PSB, corroborative documents, and religious affiliation.
propositions.quote: The Appeal gives rise to the following issues: a. Did the Panel err in finding that the Appellant could not have exited China on his own genuine passport even with the help of the smuggler? b. Did the Panel err in finding that the Appellant was not wanted by the Public Security Bureau because of the Appellant's political activities? c. Did the Panel err in assessing the Appellant's corroborative documentation and specifically, the Appellant's summons? d. Did the Panel err in its assessment of the Appellant's religious affiliation?

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies four issues on the appeal about exit, PSB wanted status, documents, and religious affiliation.

propositions.text: The appellant described family and son's medical difficulties, which improved after his wife practiced Roman Catholicism.
propositions.quote: The Appellant described his family situation and the medical difficulties with their son. When the medical difficulties were not solved by doctors, the Appellant's wife started practicing Roman Catholicism. As a result of the Appellant's wife's practice, their son's condition gradually got better.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant described family medical difficulties improving after his wife practiced Roman Catholicism.

propositions.text: The appellant declined joining the church but volunteered; the church received an expropriation letter and government tried to demolish it in June 2016.
propositions.quote: The Appellant declined his wife's offer of joining the church, but he did volunteer work when he had time. The Appellant's wife's church received an expropriation letter early in June 2016. The church members did not agree, stating that the building was located beside an area of expropriation. On June 16, 2016, government officers came with bulldozers and construction workers to try and demolish the building.

propositions.text: The appellant confronted workers, yelling that Chinese citizens had no rights.
propositions.quote: The Appellant confronted the workers, yelling at them, and stating that Chinese citizens had no rights.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant did volunteer work; government tried to demolish the church; appellant confronted workers yelling about citizens' rights.

propositions.text: After workers beat citizens, appellant hid; police accused him of illegal religious activities and protesting; PSB searched for him at homes.
propositions.quote: After the workers began beating the citizens, the Appellant escaped and went into hiding. He was informed that the police had come and accused him of being involved in illegal religious activities, and having interfered with the work of the government by taking the lead in protesting against the government. After failing to report, the Public Security Bureau (PSB) returned to his home and his relative's homes looking for him.

propositions.text: Appellant enlisted a smuggler to improperly obtain a Canadian visa and left China.
propositions.quote: As a result, the Appellant enlisted the support of a smuggler to improperly obtain a Canadian visa, and he left China on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX

paragraphs.summary: The appellant hid after police accused him; PSB searched for him; he used a smuggler to get a Canadian visa and left China.

propositions.text: After arriving in Canada, appellant learned church was torn down; PSB continued to look for him and issued a summons to report.
propositions.quote: After arriving in Canada, the Appellant learned that the church building had been torn down. The PSB continued to look for him, and a summons was issued ordering him to report to the PSB.

propositions.text: Appellant fears arrest and jail if he returns to China.
propositions.quote: The Appellant fears that if he returned to China he would be arrested and jailed.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant learned the church was demolished; PSB issued a summons; he fears arrest if returned to China.

propositions.text: RPD hearing held October 21, 2016; decision November 2, 2016, found appellant not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The RPD hearing was held on October 21, 2016, and in a decision of November 2, 2016, the RPD found that the Appellant was neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD held a hearing and decided the appellant was not a Convention refugee or person in need of protection.

propositions.text: RAD decision on March 23, 2017, upheld RPD decision denying refugee status and protection.
propositions.quote: The RPD decision was appealed to the Refugee Appeal Divison (RAD). In a decision of March 23, 2017, the RAD upheld the RPD decision and found that the Appellant was neither a Convention refugee nor person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD upheld the RPD decision denying refugee status and protection.

propositions.text: Federal Court set aside RAD decision on November 24, 2017, and remanded for re-determination by different RAD member.
propositions.quote: The RAD decision was appealed to the Federal Court and in a decision on November 24, 2017, the Hon. Mr. Justice Campbell set aside the RAD decision and sent the matter back for re-determination by a different RAD member.

paragraphs.summary: The Federal Court set aside the RAD decision and remanded for re-determination by a different RAD member.

propositions.text: Appellant supports the standard of review from FCA Huruglica decision for RAD review of RPD decisions.
propositions.quote: The Appellant was supportive of the standard of review outlined in the decision of the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) in Huruglica.1 This decision provides guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal, such as the RAD, to decisions of the first-level administrative tribunal.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant supports the Huruglica standard of review for RAD's review of RPD decisions.

propositions.text: FCA stated RAD applies correctness standard to fact and mixed fact-law findings without oral credibility issues.
propositions.quote: The FCA stated that, with respect to findings of fact (and mixed fact and law), which raised no issue of credibility of oral evidence, the RAD is to review RPD decisions by applying the correctness standard.

propositions.text: Under IRPA 111(2)(b), RAD may refer matter back to RPD if it cannot decide without hearing RPD evidence.
propositions.quote: Pursuant to paragraph 111(2)(b) of the IRPA, the RAD may refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination if it is "of the opinion" that it cannot make a decision confirming or setting aside the RPD's decision without hearing the evidence presented before the RPD.

propositions.text: Court applies correctness standard for fact, mixed fact-law, and law issues per Huruglica; applies modified reasonableness for credibility issues per X (Re).
propositions.quote: For questions of fact, mixed fact and law, and law, I have applied the standard of correctness, as per Huruglica. In assessing issues involving credibility of oral testimony, I have applied the RAD modified standard of reasonableness in those situations where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in making a particular finding, as per the decision in X (Re), 2017 CanLII 33034 (CA IRB).

propositions.text: RAD should exercise restraint before substituting its determination, decided case-by-case.
propositions.quote: It further indicates that, although the RAD should sometimes exercise a degree of restraint before substituting its own determination, the issue of whether the circumstances warrant such restraint ought to be addressed on a case-by-case basis.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the standard of review: correctness for fact and law, modified reasonableness for credibility, with case-by-case restraint.

propositions.text: RAD will assess RPD decision based on above principles.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its assessment of the RPD's decision on the basis of the principles outlined above.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD will assess the RPD decision based on the stated principles.

propositions.text: RPD doubted summons authenticity due to credibility findings and appellant's ability to leave China with genuine passport.
propositions.quote: The RPD doubted the veracity of the summons2 submitted in documentation because of credibility findings and his ability to leave China using his own travel documents.

propositions.text: RPD noted summons was single page with black ink and red stamps, lacking security features, and could be easily forged.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that the summons was a single page with black ink and red stamps, without any security features, and could easily be made by anyone anywhere.

propositions.text: RPD quoted documentation about fraudulent documents in China.
propositions.quote: The RPD quoted documentation regarding fraudulent documentation in China.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD doubted the summons authenticity due to lack of security features and appellant's ability to leave China with genuine passport.

propositions.text: Appellant argues RPD erred by reverse reasoning on summons authenticity and wanted status.
propositions.quote: Quoting Federal jurisprudence,4 the Appellant submits that the Panel erred by applying "reverse reasoning" to analyze the Appellant's summons.

propositions.text: Appellant says it is impermissible to conclude he is not wanted because he left China, then negate summons showing he is wanted.
propositions.quote: He stated that it is impermissible for the member to first commit herself to the conclusion that he is not wanted because he was able to exit China on his own genuine passport when allegedly being wanted by the PSB, and then negate the Appellant summons that he is indeed wanted by the PSB.

propositions.text: Appellant cites Ren v Canada to support his submissions.
propositions.quote: The Appellant also quoted Ren v Canada, 2015 FC 1402 to support his submissions.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant argues the RPD erred by reverse reasoning on summons and wanted status, citing Ren v Canada.

propositions.text: Appellant submits summons face shows no sign of inauthenticity and Board must address it, not dismiss due to prior credibility findings.
propositions.quote: The Appellant further submits that there was nothing on the face of the summons to suggest it was not authentic and that the Board was required to squarely address the document and not just dismiss it as a result of prior credibility findings.

propositions.text: Appellant admits using falsified documents and smuggler filled application; fleeing may require fraudulent documents without impugning credibility.
propositions.quote: The Appellant also submitted that he presented falsified documents to travel to Canada and that the smuggler filled out the application. The Appellant further submitted that when fleeing the country, fraudulent documents must sometimes be used in order to guarantee the person being persecuted safe passage and should not be used to impugn the credibility of the Appellant.

propositions.text: Appellant submits summons should not be assigned no weight.
propositions.quote: Given the above, the Appellant submits that the summons should not be assigned no weight.

paragraphs.summary: The appellant submits summons face shows no inauthenticity; fraudulent documents used fleeing should not impugn credibility; summons deserves weight.

propositions.text: RAD agrees summons should not be completely negated but finds summons fraudulent and draws negative credibility inference.
propositions.quote: Although there is Federal jurisprudence to support transferring credibility issues to other aspects of the claim, the RAD is an agreement with the Appellant that the RPD's findings were insufficient to completely negate the summons. There is also Federal jurisprudence to support that the seal could be considered as a security feature. However, the RAD finds that the Public Security Bureau summons, referenced above and submitted in documentation, is fraudulent and draws a negative credibility inference.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD agrees summons should not be fully negated but finds it fraudulent and draws negative credibility inference.

propositions.text: A government-issued summons was submitted to verify appellant was wanted by Chinese authorities.
propositions.quote: A government issued summons (zhi'an chuanhuan) was submitted to verify that Appellant was wanted by the Chinese authorities.

propositions.text: NDP documentation states summons format unchanged since 2003 and regional variations not meant to exist.
propositions.quote: In observing the NDP documentation, the RAD notes the following: "there has been no variation in the format of summonses and subpoenas since 2003 (ibid. 22 June 2013)." The documentation goes on to quote that such forms are supposed to be used throughout the country and that "regional variations are not meant to exist."

paragraphs.summary: The RAD notes a government summons was submitted and NDP documentation says summons format unchanged since 2003 with no regional variations.

propositions.text: Summons structure and format inconsistent with NDP documentation samples.
propositions.quote: Observing the summons submitted in documentation and comparing it to the samples in the NDP documentation, the RAD finds that structure and format of the summons is not consistent with the documentation.

propositions.text: Summons missing individual identifier on top left; line structure and spacing inconsistent with NDP documentation.
propositions.quote: The identifier of the individual named and located on the top left of the sample NDP summons, is missing. The structure of the second and third line are inconsistent with the NDP documentation, specifically the Chinese character before the number 30 is on the second line not the third. In observing the spacing for the bottom three lines of the document, the RAD finds that it is inconsistent with the documentation, provided in the NDP, in both location on the document and character sizing.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the summons structure, missing identifier, line structure, and spacing inconsistent with NDP documentation.

propositions.text: RAD finds Chinese characters on the Public Security Authority seal inconsistent with documentation
propositions.quote: In observing the Chinese characters where the Seal of the Public Security Authority is placed, the RAD finds that they are inconsistent with the documentation.

propositions.text: NDP documentation has 6 Chinese characters in parentheses, but submitted document has 5
propositions.quote: The NDP documentation has 6 Chinese characters enclosed by parenthesis while the document presented has 5.

propositions.text: A Chinese character indicating perpetrator's signature is missing on the summons submitted
propositions.quote: At the bottom of the document where the information for the alleged perpetrator is given, there is a Chinese character on the third line to indicate where the perpetrator is to sign. That character is missing on the summons submitted in documentation.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds inconsistencies in Chinese characters on the Public Security Authority seal and summons document compared to NDP documentation.

propositions.text: RAD finds on balance of probabilities that the summons submitted is fraudulent
propositions.quote: The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the summons submitted is fraudulent, and draws a negative inference regarding the Appellant's credibility in submitting a fraudulent document to support his case.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the summons fraudulent and negatively infers on the Appellant's credibility for submitting it.

propositions.text: Given fraudulent documentation, RAD finds Appellant was not wanted by Chinese authorities as alleged
propositions.quote: Given this fraudulent documentation, the RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant was not wanted by the PSB or the authorities in China as alleged.

propositions.text: No credible documentation supports Appellant's allegations of being wanted by authorities
propositions.quote: Given that there is no credible documentation given to support his allegations of being wanted by the authorities, the RAD finds the Appellant is not a credible witness about his allegations

propositions.text: Determinative basis of claim, being wanted for political activities, is not credible
propositions.quote: and finds that a determinative basis of his claim, i.e. being wanted by the authorities in China for his alleged political activities against the government, is not credible.

propositions.text: Appellant could have left China on own documentation without difficulty
propositions.quote: Given this finding, the RAD finds that the Appellant could have left China on his own documentation without difficulty

propositions.text: Allegations that Appellant used a smuggler to exit China are not credible
propositions.quote: and that the allegations that he used a smuggler to arrange his exit from China, are not credible.

propositions.text: Use of fraudulent info on Canadian visa application is not determinative in this claim
propositions.quote: The fact that the Appellant used fraudulent information on his Canadian visa application is not a determinative issue in this claim.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the summons fraudulent, Appellant not wanted by authorities, not credible on key allegations, and could have left China without difficulty.

propositions.text: RPD found Appellant not wanted by Chinese authorities because he exited China using own documentation
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellant was not wanted by the Chinese authorities because he was able to exit China using his own documentation.

propositions.text: RPD explained Chinese authorities' efficacy in apprehending citizens attempting to leave China
propositions.quote: The RPD explained at length the efficacy of Chinese authorities in apprehending Chinese citizens when they attempt to leave China.

propositions.text: RPD noted systematic corruption and bribery among Chinese airport officials
propositions.quote: The panel noted there was systematic corruption in China and that airport officials can be bribed and that documentary evidence indicates the authorities in China do not always apply regulations evenly.

propositions.text: RPD found preponderance of evidence shows thorough screening of passengers at airports and borders
propositions.quote: However, the RPD found that the preponderance of documentary evidence states that authorities at airports and borders conduct a thorough screening of passengers.

propositions.text: RPD preferred unbiased country conditions evidence over Appellant's testimony that he is wanted for arrest
propositions.quote: In that the Appellant testified that he is wanted for arrest, the RPD preferred the unbiased country conditions evidence to his testimony.

propositions.text: RPD found on balance of probabilities that Appellant was not wanted by Chinese authorities having exited on own identity documents
propositions.quote: The RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant was not wanted by the Chinese authorities having exited on his own identity documents.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found Appellant not wanted by Chinese authorities because he exited China on own documents despite corruption and bribery concerns.

propositions.text: Appellant submits RPD erred in finding he could not exit China on own passport if wanted by PSB
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that the RPD erred when it found that he could not have exited China on his own passport if he was wanted by the PSB.

propositions.text: Appellant submits RPD erred by preferring one type of evidence over another
propositions.quote: The Appellant further submits that the RPD erred by preferring one type of evidence over another.

propositions.text: Appellant submitted Federal jurisprudence supporting possibility of wanted person bypassing border security with own passport
propositions.quote: The Appellant submitted Federal jurisprudence to support its submission that a person could be wanted by the authorities and be able to bypass border security using their own passport.

propositions.text: Appellant references NDP documentation on endemic fraud and bribery among law enforcers
propositions.quote: The Appellant further references NDP documentation regarding the "endemic" fraud and bribery among enforcers of the law.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD erred in its findings about exit from China and evidence preference, citing Federal jurisprudence and NDP documentation.

propositions.text: Appellant submits RPD erred by not asking about smuggler support at customs
propositions.quote: The Appellant further submits that the RPD erred by not asking the Appellant about the support given to him by the smuggler when he went through customs.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues the RPD erred by not questioning him about smuggler support at customs.

propositions.text: RAD found documentation supporting Appellant was wanted by Chinese authorities was fraudulent
propositions.quote: Above in this decision, the RAD found that the documentation submitted, to support that the Appellant was wanted by the Chinese authorities, was fraudulent.

propositions.text: Appellant's testimony that he left China without difficulty supports RAD's finding of no credible wanted status
propositions.quote: The documentation and testimony of the Appellant that he was able to leave China without difficulty supports the RAD's finding above.

propositions.text: No probative documentation that Appellant was wanted by authorities; he could have left China with appropriate documentation
propositions.quote: Given that there is no probative documentation that he was wanted by the authorities, the Appellant could have left China without difficulty providing he had the appropriate documentation.

propositions.text: RAD finds on balance of probabilities that Appellant did not use a smuggler as alleged
propositions.quote: The RAD also finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant did not use a smuggler as alleged.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the documentation fraudulent, no credible wanted status, Appellant left China without difficulty, and did not use a smuggler.

propositions.text: RPD found Appellant's testimony about protest behaviour implausible and unlikely
propositions.quote: The RPD found that the Appellant's testimony about his behaviour at the alleged protest to be implausible and unlikely.

propositions.text: RPD reasoned Appellant was not church member, did not own expropriated land, and fled before PSB arrived
propositions.quote: The RPD reasoned that the Appellant was not a member of the church, did not own the land being expropriated, and that he ran away before the PSB officers arrived.

propositions.text: RPD did not accept Appellant's explanation that PSB could get info about him as reason for fleeing
propositions.quote: The RPD did not accept his explanation when the testified that the PSB could get information about him as a reason for running away.

propositions.text: RPD noted Appellant's wife was church member, participated in protest, was not arrested, and remains employed in family home
propositions.quote: The RPD further reasoned that the Appellant's wife was a member of the church, participated in the protest, was not arrested, and according to testimony she remains in the family home and continues to be employed.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found Appellant's protest testimony implausible, noting his non-membership, fleeing before PSB arrival, and wife's continued presence.

propositions.text: RPD found Appellant did not explain how he was a protest leader
propositions.quote: When questioned on his alleged leadership, the RPD found that he did not explain in any way how he was a leader as he did not plan the protest, did not write anything to the government, and his name does not appear in any related documentation.

propositions.text: RPD found Appellant had no history of protesting and would not have been permitted to leave China if perceived as threat
propositions.quote: In that the Appellant did not have a history of protesting anything, the RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that if he was perceived to be an irritant or threat to the government, he would not have been permitted to leave China.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found Appellant did not prove leadership and would not have been allowed to leave China if a government threat.

propositions.text: Appellant submits he was deeply involved as volunteer despite not being church member
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that even though he was not a member of the church congregation, he was deeply involved because of his involvement as a volunteer.

propositions.text: Appellant submits BOC narrative outlines his protest involvement
propositions.quote: The Appellant further submits that his BOC narrative outlines his involvement in the protest.

propositions.text: Appellant submits RPD did not ask questions or express concerns about this evidence
propositions.quote: He further submits that the RPD did not ask questions or express concerns regarding this aspect of the evidence.

propositions.text: Appellant submits RPD ignored relevant evidence and failed to consider plausibility of PSB identifying and arresting him
propositions.quote: He further submits that the RPD ignored relevant evidence and failed to consider the plausibility and ease with which the PSB could identify the Appellant and therefore require his arrest.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues he was deeply involved as volunteer, BOC narrative supports this, and RPD ignored relevant evidence and concerns.

propositions.text: RAD found Appellant not wanted by PSB as alleged, undermining protest leadership claims
propositions.quote: Above in this decision, the RAD found that the Appellant was not wanted by the PSB as alleged. This fact undermines the Appellant's documentation and testimony that he was involved in a protest as a leader and went into hiding.

propositions.text: RAD finds Appellant's testimony on leadership not probative and BOC narrative allegations unsubstantiated
propositions.quote: The RAD has reviewed the testimony of the Appellant regarding his alleged leadership, and finds, on a balance of probabilities, that his testimony was not probative in confirming this allegation. The allegations in the Appellant's BOC narrative have not been substantiated.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellant not wanted by PSB, undermining leadership claims, and finds his testimony and BOC narrative unsubstantiated.

propositions.text: If protest occurred, allegations of hiding and potential arrest are not credible
propositions.quote: If in fact the protest was held, as testimony and documentation attest to, the RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the ensuing allegations of hiding and potential arrest are not credible.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds that if the protest occurred, allegations of hiding and potential arrest are not credible.

propositions.text: RPD finds Appellant's name not on land expropriation documents and they do not substantiate protest participation
propositions.quote: In reviewing the documentation concerning the land expropriation, the RPD finds that the Appellant's name is not on any of these documents nor do they substantiate his assertion that he participated in a demonstration and clashed with workers there.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD finds Appellant's name absent from land expropriation documents and no proof of protest participation.

propositions.text: Appellant focused submissions on genuineness of summons, which has been addressed
propositions.quote: The Appellant, as outlined above, focused his submissions on the genuineness of the summons. That issue has been addressed above.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant focused on summons genuineness, which the RAD has already addressed.

propositions.text: RAD finds Appellant's name absent from land expropriation document and no probative info on protest or incarceration allegations
propositions.quote: In reviewing the land expropriation document submitted, the RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant's name does not appear, nor does it provide any probative information about his allegations of a protest and potential incarceration by the authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellant's name absent from land expropriation document and no probative info on protest or incarceration.

propositions.text: RPD noted Appellant testified he was not church member in China but attends church in Canada with supporting letter
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that the Appellant testified that he was not a member of the church congregation in China but that he now attends a church in Canada and provided a letter from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX to support this allegation.

propositions.text: RPD found Appellant chose church for convenience, was not baptized, and not yet practicing Catholic
propositions.quote: The RPD noted that the Appellant testified that he chose this church for the convenience of where he lived, was not yet baptized, and found, on a balance of probabilities, that he was not yet a practicing Catholic.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found Appellant not a church member in China, attends church in Canada for convenience, not baptized or practicing Catholic.

propositions.text: RPD quoted NDP documentation that Catholic Church is recognized and small house churches tolerated in China
propositions.quote: The RPD quoted NDP documentation to support that the Catholic Church is recognized by Chinese authorities and that they generally tolerate small house church groups.

propositions.text: RPD found millions of Chinese live and worship in China
propositions.quote: Further the documentation indicates that millions of Chinese live and worship in China.

propositions.text: RPD found on balance of probabilities that Appellant could worship in many congregations without attracting authorities' interest
propositions.quote: The RPD found, on a balance of probabilities, that should he wish to worship on his return to China, there are many congregations he could attend without attracting the interest of authorities.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found Catholic Church recognized and tolerated in China; Appellant could worship without attracting authorities' interest.

propositions.text: Appellant submits he provided sufficient evidence of religious identity and participation, and RPD erred doubting his practice
propositions.quote: The Appellant submits that he provided sufficient evidence to establish his religious identity and that he regularly participates in church activities, has knowledge of Christianity, and has pictures of himself at church practicing his religion. He submits that the RPD erred by doubting the genuineness of his practice because of his testimony regarding the geographical proximity of the church he attends.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues he provided sufficient evidence of religious identity and participation, and RPD erred doubting his practice.

propositions.text: Appellant submits RPD erred stating he could choose any church in China, citing NDP documentation on Patriotic church nonrecognition
propositions.quote: Referencing Federal jurisprudence, the Appellant submits that the RPD erred when it stated that the Appellant could choose any number of churches upon his return to China. The NDP documentation indicates that the Pope is not recognized by the Patriotic church in China and this nonrecognition constitutes significant doctrinal differences.

propositions.text: Appellant submits serious restrictions include arrest, detention, and limits on public practice, preaching, and religious instruction
propositions.quote: He submits that serious restrictions are not limited to arrest and detention but restrictions in the ability to practice in public, preach, and had the benefits of religious instruction and leadership.

paragraphs.summary: The Appellant argues RPD erred ignoring serious restrictions on religious practice due to Patriotic church nonrecognition.

propositions.text: RAD finds Appellant could return to China without fear of persecution
propositions.quote: The RAD has reviewed all of the documentation in this case and finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant could return to China without fear of persecution.

propositions.text: Appellant's wife practices Roman Catholicism in China without persecution or fear
propositions.quote: His wife, according to documentation and testimony, practices Roman Catholicism in China without any persecution or fear from the Chinese authorities.

propositions.text: Appellant began religious practice in Canada, was not baptized or official member at RPD hearing, but showed interest
propositions.quote: The Appellant has begun his religious practice in Canada and although he was not yet baptized or officially a member of the Roman Catholic Church at the time of the RPD hearing, he has indicated, according to the letter submitted, an interest in pursuing this religion.

propositions.text: Letter dated October 20, 2016 states Appellant was to complete program by July 8, 2017 Parish Day
propositions.quote: The RAD notes that this letter was dated October 20, 2016, and states that he was to have successfully completed the program as of July 8, 2017, Parish Day.

propositions.text: No additional documentation submitted on appeal confirming continued practice or baptism
propositions.quote: No additional documentation was submitted on appeal to confirm that the Appellant has continued this practice of Roman Catholicism or has been baptized.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds Appellant could return to China without persecution; his wife practices Catholicism freely; he began practice in Canada but no proof of baptism.

propositions.text: The Appellant could return to China without fear of persecution and continue practicing his religion with his wife.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant could return to China without fear of persecution and continue, with his wife, the practice of his newfound religion.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD finds the Appellant can return to China without fear of persecution and continue his religious practice with his wife.

propositions.text: The RAD confirms the RPD's decision and dismisses the appeal under paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.
propositions.quote: The RAD confirms the RPD's determination and dismisses the appeal according to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.

propositions.text: The Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
propositions.quote: The RAD finds that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee, nor person in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD confirms the RPD's decision, dismisses the appeal, and finds the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor in need of protection.
